title: Detection of Search Victim-Owned Websites
summary: This strategy detects searches of victim owned websites, ATT&CK technique T1594, where an adversary browses the organisation's public sites to collect employee names, email addresses, technology details, support procedures and anything sensitive that was published by mistake. The telemetry is on the victim's own infrastructure, which makes this one of the few reconnaissance techniques that can be detected with confidence: web server and reverse proxy logs record each request with path, status code, user agent and client address, and a web application firewall logs the same traffic with attack and enumeration context. The pattern is methodical collection rather than browsing, for example a single client requesting many pages of one section in a short window, walking staff directories in numeric order, retrieving backup or configuration file extensions, or reading the published sitemap and then requesting pages outside it. Noise comes from search engine crawlers, uptime monitors, marketing analytics and content editors, all of which look similar. The strategy fails when logs are not retained long enough to see a campaign, when a web application firewall blocks a probe and therefore hides it from the analyst, and when the traffic is spread across many source addresses.

beginner.definition: Your company website is public, so anyone may read it. Some people read it in a way that shows they are collecting information, not shopping or reading news. This detection studies your web server logs for that behaviour. It looks for one visitor walking through many pages or staff listings in a short time.
beginner.whyItMatters: Public pages often leak more than intended. A staff page lists names and roles. A support page describes internal tools. A public upload folder can hold documents that were never meant to be shared. An attacker who reads all of it can build a believable story for a phishing message. The request log is the only place this behaviour is visible, and it is already being recorded. Reviewing it turns a quiet research walk into an early warning.
howItWorks: Your web server writes a log line for every request. Each line has the page, the visitor address, the browser name and the result code.
The rule counts how many different pages one visitor reads in a short window.
It looks for signs of a walk, such as staff pages visited in order, or addresses with numbers that climb.
It also checks for requests to file types that should never be public, such as backups or configuration files.
Known search engine crawlers and your own monitoring tools are removed from the count.
Visitors whose pattern looks like collection are grouped and raised with the pages they read.
beginner.example: Think of a shop with an open notice board. Most visitors read one or two notices and leave. One visitor stands there for twenty minutes. They copy every notice into a notebook. That includes the staff rota and the delivery schedule. Nothing was stolen and no lock was broken. But the shopkeeper would want to know about it. That notebook makes a burglary much easier to plan. Your web log is the record of who stood at the board.
takeaways: You can detect this reconnaissance, because the search happens on your own servers and is logged.
The signal is the pattern of a walk, not a single unusual page.
Look for mistakes too: public backup and configuration files are worse than any search.

objectives: Explain how public website content supports later phishing and intrusion activity
Identify the web server and web application firewall fields needed to detect methodical collection
Build a request volume and breadth baseline per client address and user agent
Detect directory walking, sequential identifier enumeration and requests for non public file types
Recognise crawler, monitoring and content editor traffic that resembles collection
Feed website reconnaissance findings into exposure review and content clean up
dataSources: Web server access logs containing client address, requested path, query string, status code, user agent and response size
Web application firewall or reverse proxy logs capturing blocked and allowed requests with attack classification
Robots exclusion file and sitemap access records showing whether discovery files were fetched before content crawling
Content management system audit logs recording page listing and media library browsing by authenticated editors
Asset inventory of public hostnames and published document repositories used to identify paths that should never be requested
logic: The detection measures collection behaviour rather than individual requests. It aggregates web requests by client address and user agent over a window, then looks at three properties: breadth, meaning the number of distinct paths requested, depth, meaning how far into a single section or numeric identifier range the client walks, and content type, meaning requests for extensions or directories that are not linked from the public site. Supporting correlation comes from robots exclusion and sitemap fetches, because a client that reads the discovery files and then requests unlinked paths is following a deliberate collection plan rather than browsing. The benign case is a search engine crawler with a verifiable user agent, an uptime monitor requesting a fixed small path set, or a content editor authenticated into the content management system and previewing pages. The malicious case is a client with a generic or blank user agent requesting many unlinked paths, walking sequential identifiers, or requesting archives and configuration files, and the response codes show the attacker probing rather than finding.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Methodical Content Collection Against Public Website
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: webserver
# detection:
#   selection:
#     cs_method: GET
#     sc_status: 200
#   filter_crawlers:
#     cs_user_agent|contains:
#       - 'Googlebot'
#       - 'Bingbot'
#       - 'UptimeRobot'
#   filter_assets:
#     cs_uri_stem|endswith:
#       - '.css'
#       - '.js'
#       - '.png'
#   condition: selection and not filter_crawlers and not filter_assets
# level: low
falsePositives: Search engine and partner crawlers that index the public site and are identified by a verifiable user agent or reverse lookup
Uptime and performance monitoring services that request a small fixed set of pages every minute
Marketing analytics and link preview bots that fetch pages when a link is shared in a message or on a social platform
Content editors, translators and accessibility auditors reviewing published pages through the content management system
tuningNotes: Set the alert on distinct paths per client per ten minute window rather than on total requests, because a single heavy page with many images can otherwise dominate the count, and exclude static asset extensions from the count. Maintain a crawler allow list by user agent plus reverse domain name system verification, since user agent strings are trivial to copy. Scope the first release to paths that are never linked publicly, such as staff directories, upload folders and archived document trees, and leave the general site at a lower threshold. Narrowing to unlinked paths costs you visibility into an attacker who only reads linked pages at a deliberate pace, so keep a longer horizon statistic that flags a client returning daily to the same section over a week.
